set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: The raised yellow-white plaques shown line a patient's colon. Which organism produces them?
set1.alt: Colonoscopy view of pink colon lining dotted with raised yellow-white plaques, two of them marked with arrows.
opts: Bacillus cereus
Bacillus cereus causes a 24-hour toxin illness of vomiting or diarrhea without colonic plaques.
Clostridioides difficile
Correct: these are the pseudomembranes of antibiotic-associated colitis, sloughed necrotic intestinal lining.
Clostridium perfringens
Clostridium perfringens causes a mild, rapidly resolving gastroenteritis, not pseudomembranous colitis.
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria is often mild in healthy adults and affects the brain and meninges in vulnerable patients rather than forming colonic plaques.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 47

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: In vulnerable patients, what does Listeria monocytogenes infection affect?
opts: The brain and meninges
Correct: in immunocompromised patients, fetuses and neonates it affects the brain and meninges.
The heart valves
Endocarditis is linked here to Actinomyces viscosus, not to listeriosis.
The wall of the colon
Damage to the colon wall is the work of Clostridioides difficile enterotoxins.
The peripheral nerves
Peripheral nerve damage, in Schwann cells, is the hallmark of leprosy.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 55

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What is iatrogenic botulism?
opts: Toxin made by spores growing in a wound
Spores growing in a wound and making toxin is wound botulism.
Toxin from spores colonizing an adult gut
Toxin from intestinal colonization in someone over age 1 is intestinal colonization botulism.
Paralysis from eating home-canned food
Eating preformed toxin in home-canned food is foodborne botulism.
Illness from medical use of the toxin
Correct: it occurs when cosmetic or therapeutic procedures that use botulinum toxin cause systemic intoxication.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which contaminated product has caused Bacillus cereus sepsis at injection sites?
opts: Black tar heroin
Black tar heroin is associated with wound botulism in people who inject drugs.
Raw cow's milk
Raw cow's milk carries Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis rather than Bacillus cereus sepsis.
Alcohol prep pads
Correct: rare infections have been traced to contaminated alcohol prep pads, producing clinical sepsis from contaminated injection sites.
Honey pacifiers
Honey pacifiers were linked to infant botulism rather than to Bacillus cereus sepsis.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Judging by where the spores sit in the rods shown, which genus are they?
set1.alt: Stained rods containing spores on a yellow background, high magnification.
opts: Bacillus
The Bacillus anthracis spore sits in the center of the cell without swelling it, rather than at one end as these do.
Lactobacillus
Lactobacillus forms no spores; it is a regular, uniformly staining rod of the normal flora.
Corynebacterium
Corynebacterium forms no spores; it is pleomorphic, with granules and palisades rather than terminal swellings.
Clostridium
Correct: the spores swell one end of each rod, the terminal spores of Clostridium tetani with its drumstick shape.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 28

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Why is pulmonary anthrax called woolsorters' disease?
opts: Sorters swallow spores from their hands
Swallowed spores in meat cause gastrointestinal anthrax; woolsorters' disease is acquired by inhalation.
Sheep transmit the bacillus by biting
Anthrax is a zoonosis acquired from spores, not by animal bites; woolsorters inhale spores from the wool.
Sorters inhale spores from infected wool
Correct: it is acquired by inhaling spores from infected animal products or soil, so people handling wool from infected sheep were exposed.
Wool fibers cut the skin and let spores in
Spores entering through cuts cause cutaneous anthrax; woolsorters' disease is the inhaled, pulmonary form.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which form of anthrax is the most deadly?
opts: Injection
Injection anthrax spreads faster than the cutaneous form, but the most deadly form is pulmonary anthrax.
Pulmonary
Correct: untreated pulmonary anthrax (woolsorters' disease) is almost always fatal within about three days of the first symptoms.
Cutaneous
Cutaneous anthrax is the most common form and the least lethal, healing to an eschar in most treated patients.
Gastrointestinal
Gastrointestinal anthrax is serious, and most patients survive with aggressive treatment; pulmonary anthrax is the deadliest.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 13

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How does botulinum toxin cause paralysis?
opts: It blocks acetylcholine release
Correct: botulin is carried to neuromuscular junctions and blocks the release of acetylcholine, which is needed for muscle contraction.
It blocks inhibitory transmitters in the cord
Blocking the inhibitory transmitters gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine is tetanospasmin, which causes spasm.
It destroys myelin on peripheral nerves
Botulin leaves the nerve intact; it blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.
It lyses motor neurons in the spinal cord
Botulin does not kill motor neurons; it blocks acetylcholine release where they meet the muscle.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 35

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which stain is used on sputum to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
opts: A Gram stain alone
Mycobacteria do not Gram stain well because of the waxes and mycolic acids in the wall; sputum is stained acid-fast.
Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain
Correct: sputum is stained acid-fast by Ziehl-Neelsen or by a fluorescent acid-fast method, alongside culture and nucleic acid probes.
Alkaline methylene blue
Alkaline methylene blue is the stain used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
A spore stain with heat
Mycobacteria form no spores; their stain is the acid-fast Ziehl-Neelsen method.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 77

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What usually causes death in tetanus?
opts: Septic shock from cytokine release
Shock from a cytokine flood is the picture of severe anthrax rather than tetanus.
Perforation of the colon
Colon perforation is a complication of Clostridioides difficile disease.
Asphyxiation by a throat membrane
Asphyxiation by a throat pseudomembrane is the danger in respiratory diphtheria.
Respiratory muscle paralysis
Correct: death most often comes from paralysis of the respiratory muscles.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Why was secondary tuberculosis called consumption?
opts: Patients wasted away
Correct: violent coughing, greenish or bloody sputum, fever, anorexia, weight loss and fatigue made patients waste away.
Patients consumed too much milk
The name comes from wasting; raw milk is linked to Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis.
The bacilli consumed the ribs
Spread to long bones is extrapulmonary tuberculosis; consumption refers to the wasting of secondary disease.
It spread through shared food
Tuberculosis spreads by airborne droplets; consumption refers to wasting.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 74

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which findings support a diagnosis of leprosy?
opts: Watery diarrhea after antibiotics
Diarrhea after antibiotics points to Clostridioides difficile.
A painless papule turning black
A painless papule becoming a black eschar is cutaneous anthrax.
Numb skin with acid-fast bacilli
Correct: numbness, loss of heat and cold sensitivity, thickened earlobes and a chronic stuffy nose, with acid-fast bacilli in lesions or nasal discharge.
A pseudomembrane and myocarditis
A pseudomembrane with myocarditis is respiratory diphtheria with toxemia.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 87

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What is the primary reservoir of Listeria monocytogenes?
opts: Human sebaceous glands
Pilosebaceous glands are home to Cutibacterium acnes, the acne organism.
Soil, water and animal intestines
Correct: its primary reservoir is soil and water, along with animal intestines, from which it contaminates food.
The throats of healthy carriers
Healthy human carriers are the reservoir of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
The tonsils of healthy pigs
The tonsils of healthy pigs are the reservoir of Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 55

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which condition produces the facial lesions shown?
set1.alt: Close view of a man's face with skin lesions.
opts: Cervicofacial actinomycosis
Cervicofacial actinomycosis follows an oral infection, near the jaw, rather than nodules across the face.
Lepromatous leprosy
Correct: deep, disfiguring nodules of the face are lepromatous leprosy, the widely disseminated form.
Tuberculoid leprosy
Tuberculoid leprosy gives shallow, asymmetrical lesions with local loss of pain sensation, not deep nodules.
Cutaneous anthrax
Cutaneous anthrax produces a single black necrotic eschar after a painless papule.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 86

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How does Bacillus cereus most commonly make people ill?
opts: Through contact with armadillos
Armadillos are a possible zoonotic source of leprosy, not of Bacillus cereus.
Through contaminated food
Correct: it is most commonly a foodborne illness; its spores are very commonly airborne and dustborne and land on foods.
Through deep puncture wounds
Deep puncture wounds are the classic route for Clostridium tetani and for the gas gangrene organisms.
Through respiratory droplets
Respiratory droplets spread Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than Bacillus cereus.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What kind of vaccine is the human anthrax vaccine, Biothrax?
opts: Live spores
Live spores, with toxoid, are used to protect livestock rather than people.
A killed whole-cell vaccine
The human vaccine contains no whole cells; it is a purified toxoid.
A polysaccharide conjugate
The anthrax capsule is polypeptide, not polysaccharide, and the human vaccine is a purified toxoid.
A purified toxoid
Correct: Biothrax is a purified toxoid, given to high-risk occupations and military personnel.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 16

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What separates true myonecrosis from anaerobic cellulitis?
opts: Gas forms only in true myonecrosis
Anaerobic cellulitis also has gas and tissue damage; the difference is that it remains localized.
Anaerobic cellulitis stays painless
Pain is not the distinguishing feature; anaerobic cellulitis stays localized, while true myonecrosis spreads.
A different genus causes each one
Both are clostridial wound infections; they differ in extent, localized against spreading.
Spreading necrosis with fever
Correct: true myonecrosis spreads from the local infection with fever, tachycardia and blackened necrotic tissue, whereas anaerobic cellulitis stays localized.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 26

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: In the scheme for differentiating Gram-positive bacilli, which genus is an obligately anaerobic spore-former?
opts: Listeria
Listeria forms no spores; it sits with Erysipelothrix among the regular non-spore-formers that stain uniformly.
Corynebacterium
Corynebacterium forms no spores; it is an irregular, non-acid-fast bacillus alongside Cutibacterium.
Clostridium
Correct: the spore-formers divide into the aerobic or facultatively anaerobic Bacillus and the obligately anaerobic Clostridium.
Bacillus
Bacillus is the spore-former that is aerobic or facultatively anaerobic, the other branch from Clostridium.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 5

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which wall components make mycobacteria acid-fast?
opts: Mycolic acids and waxes
Correct: mycolic acids and waxes in the wall make them acid-fast, so heat is needed to drive the stain in and they do not Gram stain well.
A polypeptide capsule
Mycobacteria form no capsules; the polypeptide capsule belongs to Bacillus anthracis.
Terminal endospores
Mycobacteria form no spores; their acid-fastness comes from mycolic acids and waxes.
A thin peptidoglycan only
Acid-fastness comes from the mycolic acids and waxes layered into the wall.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 67

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How does infant botulism arise?
opts: Ingested spores germinate in the gut
Correct: the infant swallows spores, which germinate and release toxin in the immature gut, causing floppy baby syndrome.
Preformed toxin is eaten in canned food
Eating toxin already made in improperly canned food is foodborne botulism rather than the infant form.
Spores enter through the umbilical stump
Spores entering the umbilical stump cause neonatal tetanus rather than botulism.
Toxin crosses the placenta
Infant botulism is acquired after birth by swallowing spores, not across the placenta.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 38

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: The gray-white membrane shown covers the back of a child's throat. Which organism produces it?
set1.alt: An open mouth with a tongue depressor; a thick, off-white membrane coats the back of the throat.
opts: Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria causes mild fever, diarrhea and sore throat in healthy adults, without a pseudomembrane.
Actinomyces israelii
Actinomyces israelii causes chronic cervicofacial disease after oral infection, not a throat membrane.
Bacillus anthracis
Bacillus anthracis causes ulcers of the mouth and esophagus in gastrointestinal anthrax, not a pseudomembrane.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Correct: a pseudomembrane with swelling over the throat is indicative of respiratory diphtheria.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 63

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Besides antibiotics, what is pulmonary anthrax treated with?
opts: Fecal microbiota transplant
Fecal microbiota transplant restores colonic flora in Clostridioides difficile infection.
Surgical removal of the lung
Surgery is not the added treatment; pulmonary anthrax is given antitoxin to neutralize the toxins.
Neutralizing antitoxin
Correct: pulmonary anthrax is also treated with antitoxin, aimed at the toxins that drive its shock.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Hyperbaric oxygen floods tissue with oxygen to inhibit the anaerobe of gas gangrene rather than treating anthrax.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 16

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which organism most commonly causes gas gangrene?
opts: Clostridium perfringens
Correct: Clostridium perfringens is the most common cause of myonecrosis (gas gangrene), though Clostridium novyi and Clostridium septicum can also cause it.
Clostridium tetani
Clostridium tetani causes tetanus, a neuromuscular disease, rather than gas gangrene.
Clostridium botulinum
Clostridium botulinum causes botulism, a paralytic intoxication, rather than gas gangrene.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis rather than gas gangrene.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How do newborns in developing countries acquire tetanus?
opts: Honey in their feeds
Honey is associated with infant botulism, the flaccid floppy baby syndrome, rather than tetanus.
The placenta
The organism does not cross the placenta; neonatal tetanus enters through the umbilical stump.
The umbilical stump
Correct: spores entering the umbilical stump cause neonatal tetanus, which is why it is seen in developing countries.
Their mother's milk
Tetanus is not carried in breast milk; neonates are infected through the umbilical stump.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How is diphtheria prevented?
opts: Pasteurization and thorough cooking
Pasteurization and cooking prevent listeriosis, a foodborne infection.
Antitoxin given to every newborn
Antitoxin treats established respiratory diphtheria; prevention is the toxoid vaccine series.
Live attenuated bovine bacilli
An attenuated Mycobacterium bovis strain is the tuberculosis vaccine used in other countries.
Toxoid vaccine and boosters
Correct: a toxoid vaccine series (from 6 to 8 weeks, at 15 months and at school age) with boosters prevents it.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 64

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Abdominal actinomycosis can follow which event?
opts: An intrauterine device
Intrauterine devices lead to uterine actinomycosis rather than the abdominal form.
A swimming pool scrape
A pool scrape is linked to Mycobacterium marinum granuloma, not actinomycosis.
A burst appendix
Correct: abdominal actinomycosis is a complication of a burst appendix, gunshot wounds or ulcers.
An oral infection
An oral infection leads to cervicofacial actinomycosis rather than the abdominal form.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 93

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What happens in secondary tuberculosis?
opts: Tubercles drain into the bronchi
Correct: reactivated bacilli expand the tubercles, which drain into the bronchial tubes and upper respiratory tract as symptoms worsen.
Tubercles heal quietly by calcification
Healing by calcification is the course of primary tuberculosis when it resolves.
Bacilli grow in skin and Schwann cells
Growth in skin macrophages and Schwann cells is Mycobacterium leprae.
Toxin from the lung blocks acetylcholine
The tubercle bacillus has no exotoxin; blocking acetylcholine is botulinum toxin.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 74

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What is the current name of Propionibacterium acnes?
opts: Cutibacterium acnes
Correct: the genus Propionibacterium has been reclassified as Cutibacterium, so the acne organism is Cutibacterium acnes.
Corynebacterium acnes
Corynebacterium is a separate irregular genus, home of Corynebacterium diphtheriae; the new name is Cutibacterium acnes.
Clostridioides acnes
Clostridioides is the new genus for the spore-forming difficile organism; the acne organism is Cutibacterium acnes.
Actinomyces acnes
Actinomyces is a filamentous genus; Propionibacterium acnes is now Cutibacterium acnes.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 65

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which complication belongs to Clostridioides difficile disease?
opts: Descending paralysis
Descending paralysis is the pattern of botulism, from blocked acetylcholine release.
Toxic megacolon
Correct: it causes antibiotic-associated (pseudomembranous) colitis, toxic megacolon and perforation of the colon.
Myocarditis
Myocarditis with an abnormal electrocardiogram is a target-organ effect of diphtheria toxin.
Meningitis
Meningitis can complicate any form of anthrax and is a risk of listeriosis in vulnerable patients.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 43

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: What is the primary habitat of the genus Bacillus?
opts: Sebaceous glands
Pilosebaceous glands are home to Cutibacterium acnes rather than to Bacillus.
Soil
Correct: Bacillus is mostly saprobic, degrades complex macromolecules and lives primarily in soil.
The human colon
The colon is home to Clostridioides difficile in low numbers, not the primary habitat of Bacillus.
Pig tonsils
The tonsils of healthy pigs are the reservoir of Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae rather than of Bacillus.
set1.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why does so little exposure suffice to cause primary tuberculosis?
opts: The infectious dose is about 10 cells
Correct: an infectious dose of about 10 cells, spread by respiratory droplets, is why tuberculosis transmits so readily.
The bacilli form spores in the air
Mycobacteria form no spores; their danger is a tiny infectious dose.
The bacilli multiply in stored food
Multiplication in stored food is Listeria; tuberculosis spreads by droplets with a dose of about 10 cells.
The bacilli secrete a potent exotoxin
The tubercle bacillus produces no exotoxins; a dose of about 10 cells is enough to infect.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 73

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How is gastrointestinal anthrax acquired?
opts: By inhaling spores from animal hides
Inhaling spores from animal products causes pulmonary anthrax, the most deadly form.
By injecting contaminated heroin
Contaminated heroin causes injection anthrax, an infection of the deep muscle at the injection site.
By eating infected animal meat
Correct: ingestion of contaminated meat leads to ulceration of the mouth and esophagus and localized lymphadenopathy.
By drinking water containing spores
Gastrointestinal anthrax is acquired by eating contaminated meat rather than from drinking water.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What is the lesion shown on this man's jaw and neck?
set2.alt: Two views of a lesion on a man's jaw and neck.
opts: The nodules of lepromatous leprosy
Lepromatous leprosy produces many deep nodules that disfigure the face, not a single black crusted lesion like this one.
A pseudomembrane of diphtheria
The diphtheria pseudomembrane forms in the throat from solidified inflammatory fluid, not as a black crust on the neck.
The eschar of cutaneous anthrax
Correct: a black necrotic eschar over red, swollen skin is the end stage of cutaneous anthrax, which begins as a painless papule where spores enter a cut.
The blackened tissue of gas gangrene
Gas gangrene follows deep, dirty wounds with dead tissue and spreads with gas through muscle rather than forming a single crusted eschar.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What does the test shown check for?
set2.alt: A health worker touches a feather to the skin of a boy's arm while the boy looks away.
opts: Allergy to bird proteins
The feather is a touch stimulus, testing sensation in suspected leprosy, not an allergen.
Descending weakness from botulism
Botulism produces descending paralysis; the feather test checks sensation for leprosy.
Loss of skin sensation from leprosy
Correct: this is the feather test, a low-cost way to find the numb skin and lost sensation of leprosy.
Delayed reaction to tuberculin
The tuberculin (Mantoux) test injects purified protein derivative and reads induration at 48 to 72 hours.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 88

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does a mixed infection help myonecrosis develop?
opts: Aerobes use up the oxygen
Correct: aerobic bacteria in the wound consume the oxygen, producing the low oxygen tension the anaerobic spores need to germinate and grow.
Aerobes supply toxins the anaerobe lacks
Clostridium perfringens makes its own toxins; the aerobic partners matter because they use up oxygen.
Aerobes digest tissue so spores can enter
The partners' role is to consume oxygen; Clostridium perfringens spreads through tissue with its own enzymes.
Two organisms are needed to form the gas
The gas comes from Clostridium perfringens fermenting muscle carbohydrate; the aerobes lower the oxygen tension.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What may an established Cutibacterium acnes implant infection require?
opts: Fecal microbiota transplant
Fecal microbiota transplant is for Clostridioides difficile, not implant infections.
Hyperbaric oxygen alone
Hyperbaric oxygen is used in gas gangrene; implant infection needs hardware removal and debridement.
Hardware removal and debridement
Correct: the hardware may need to come out with aggressive debridement, followed by prolonged courses of antibiotics.
A single dose of antitoxin
Cutibacterium acnes is nontoxigenic, so antitoxin has no role in treating it.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 66

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Who is most at risk of severe listeriosis?
opts: Fetuses, neonates, the immunocompromised
Correct: in these groups it affects the brain and meninges and causes fetal loss and newborn deaths, while healthy adults usually have mild illness.
Healthy young adults after a large meal
In healthy adults listeriosis is often mild or subclinical, with fever, diarrhea and sore throat.
Farmers who handle livestock daily
Pig handlers are at risk of Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae; severe listeriosis strikes the immunocompromised, fetuses and neonates.
Metal workers who inhale welding fumes
Welders are the group affected by welder's anthrax, caused by Bacillus cereus.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 55

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which T helper cell response tends to favor lepromatous leprosy?
opts: Cytotoxic T cell
The form is linked to which T helper cells predominate; T helper 2 favors lepromatous leprosy.
Regulatory T cell
The form is linked to the T helper balance: T helper 1 tuberculoid, T helper 2 lepromatous.
T helper 2
Correct: a T helper 2 response tends to favor the lepromatous form, while T helper 1 favors the tuberculoid form.
T helper 1
A T helper 1 response tends to favor the tuberculoid form, with normal T-cell responsiveness.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 84

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment lead to Clostridioides difficile disease?
opts: It kills the competing flora
Correct: the organism is a low-number, relatively non-invasive colon resident; killing the other bacteria lets it overgrow and make enterotoxins.
It makes the organism invade the colon wall
The organism is relatively non-invasive; the damage comes from enterotoxins after it overgrows.
It carries resistant spores into the gut
The organism is already a normal colon resident in low numbers; antibiotics remove its competitors.
It switches on toxin in all gut bacteria
Only Clostridioides difficile makes these enterotoxins, once antibiotics have cleared its competitors.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 42

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which food is a classic source of infant botulism?
opts: Honey
Correct: infant botulism may be associated with honey or homemade baby food; honey pacifiers caused cases in 2018.
Breast milk
Breast milk is not a described source; honey and homemade baby food are.
Fresh fruit
Fresh fruit is not a described source; infant botulism is linked to honey and homemade baby food.
Cooked rice
Cooked, reheated rice is linked to Bacillus cereus food poisoning rather than infant botulism.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Into which three divisions is clinical tuberculosis divided?
opts: Acute, subacute and chronic
Clinical tuberculosis is divided into primary, secondary and disseminated rather than by tempo.
Tuberculoid, lepromatous and mixed
Tuberculoid and lepromatous are the two polar forms of leprosy, not divisions of tuberculosis.
Cutaneous, pulmonary and intestinal
Cutaneous, pulmonary and gastrointestinal are forms of anthrax rather than divisions of tuberculosis.
Primary, secondary and disseminated
Correct: primary tuberculosis, secondary (reactivation or reinfection) tuberculosis, and disseminated (extrapulmonary) tuberculosis.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 72

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What syndrome does the infant shown illustrate?
set2.alt: An infant held face down by an adult.
opts: Floppy baby syndrome
Correct: the limp infant is infant botulism, flaccid paralysis from toxin released after ingested spores germinate in the gut.
Neonatal tetanus
Neonatal tetanus produces a rigid, arched infant, the spastic opposite of the limp baby shown.
Neonatal listeriosis
Listeriosis in newborns affects the brain and meninges rather than producing this limp, flaccid paralysis.
Diphtheritic paralysis
Diphtheria toxin can cause weakness, but diphtheria occurs in unimmunized children with a throat pseudomembrane.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why can rice that was cooked and then reheated still cause Bacillus cereus illness?
opts: It needs a sealed, low-acid can
A sealed, low-acid, home-canned food is the setting for Clostridium botulinum.
Its spores survive cooking
Correct: Bacillus cereus grows in rice, potatoes and meat, and its spores survive both cooking and reheating.
It grows only during refrigeration
Growth during refrigeration is the trait of Listeria monocytogenes, which forms no spores.
Its toxin forms only in the intestine
Toxin made in the intestine after eating is Clostridium perfringens gastroenteritis, not the Bacillus cereus emetic form.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which structures do mycobacteria lack?
opts: Cell walls and ribosomes
Mycobacteria have cell walls, rich in mycolic acids and waxes, and ribosomes like any bacterium.
Mycolic acids and waxes
Mycolic acids and waxes are what mycobacteria have; they are the basis of acid-fastness.
Catalase and cord factor
Mycobacteria produce catalase, and cord factor is a Mycobacterium tuberculosis virulence factor.
Capsules, flagella and spores
Correct: mycobacteria form no capsules, flagella or spores; they are slow-growing, catalase-positive strict aerobes.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 67

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which antibiotic is produced by members of the genus Bacillus?
opts: Dapsone
Dapsone appears here as a leprosy drug; the Bacillus products include bacitracin, gramicidin and subtilin.
Bacitracin
Correct: Bacillus produces gramicidin, tyrocidine, bacitracin, mycobacillin, surfactin, bacilysin and subtilin.
Vancomycin
Vancomycin appears here as a treatment for severe Clostridioides difficile infection rather than as a Bacillus product.
Streptomycin
Streptomycin appears here among the tuberculosis drugs rather than among the antibiotics Bacillus produces.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which spore positions distinguish Bacillus anthracis from Clostridium tetani?
opts: Terminal in Bacillus anthracis, central in Clostridium tetani
This reverses the pair: the Bacillus anthracis spore sits in the middle of the cell and the Clostridium tetani spore at one end.
Central in both, but larger in Clostridium tetani
The two differ in position, not just size: the Bacillus anthracis spore is central and the Clostridium tetani spore is terminal.
Terminal in both Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium tetani
The Clostridium tetani spore is terminal, but the Bacillus anthracis spore sits in the center of the vegetative cell.
Central in Bacillus anthracis, terminal in Clostridium tetani
Correct: Bacillus anthracis carries a centrally located spore, while the spore of Clostridium tetani swells one end of the rod, the drumstick shape.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does Listeria monocytogenes avoid the humoral immune system?
opts: It secretes a toxin that destroys antibody
Listeria's virulence is intracellular replication after inducing phagocytosis, not an antibody-destroying toxin.
It replicates inside host cells
Correct: it induces phagocytosis and then replicates in the cytoplasm of cells, out of reach of antibody.
It is coated in a thick capsule
Listeria has no capsule; its protection is replicating inside the cytoplasm of host cells.
It hides as dormant spores in tissue
Listeria forms no spores; it avoids antibody by living inside host cells.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 53

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why do so few wounds carrying Clostridium perfringens develop myonecrosis?
opts: Most wounds carry strains that lack spores
The organism forms spores readily; disease depends on host factors, dead tissue and low oxygen.
Vaccination protects most of the population
No vaccine against myonecrosis is available; disease depends on dead tissue and anaerobic conditions.
It is killed rapidly by skin bacteria
Other bacteria help rather than hinder it, by using up oxygen in a mixed infection.
It needs dead tissue and low oxygen
Correct: it is not highly invasive, so although most contaminated wounds carry it, disease needs damaged, dead tissue and anaerobic conditions.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: The newborn shown is held rigid and arched. Which toxin produces this picture?
set2.alt: A newborn held by an adult, its whole body rigidly arched backward with the head thrown back.
opts: Anthrax lethal factor
Anthrax lethal factor lyses macrophages and can cause shock; it does not cause rigid muscle spasms.
Tetanospasmin
Correct: rigid, arched spasms in a newborn are neonatal tetanus, the umbilical stump infection seen in developing countries.
Botulinum toxin
Botulinum toxin produces a limp, floppy infant with flaccid paralysis rather than rigid arching.
Diphtheria toxin
Diphtheria toxin targets the heart and nerves, causing myocarditis and weakness rather than rigid spasms.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: In Clostridium perfringens gastroenteritis, where is the toxin produced?
opts: In the food, before it is eaten
Toxin preformed in food is the pattern of botulism; Clostridium perfringens makes its toxin in the intestine.
In the liver, after absorption
The toxin is produced in the intestine and acts on intestinal epithelial cells.
In the bloodstream, after invasion
Clostridium perfringens gastroenteritis is not invasive; the toxin forms in the intestine and recovery is rapid.
In the intestine, after eating
Correct: spores surviving inadequate cooking germinate in the food, and once eaten the toxin is produced in the intestine, acting on epithelial cells.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 41

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What does tetanospasmin block the release of?
opts: Histamine from tissue mast cells
Histamine release from mast cells is an allergic mechanism; tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine
Correct: the neurotoxin blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine from spinal neurons, so muscles contract uncontrollably.
Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction is botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid paralysis.
Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves
Tetanospasmin targets the inhibitory transmitters gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine, not norepinephrine.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 29

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How is tuberculosis transmitted?
opts: Airborne respiratory droplets
Correct: the very resistant bacillus is transmitted by airborne respiratory droplets.
Improperly home-canned foods
Improperly home-canned foods carry the toxin of Clostridium botulinum, a foodborne intoxication rather than tuberculosis.
Accidental puncture wounds
Puncture wounds introduce Clostridium tetani and the gas gangrene organisms.
Handling infected armadillos
Armadillos are a possible zoonotic source of leprosy, not tuberculosis.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 71

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What produces the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning?
opts: A large molecular weight protein
A large molecular weight protein toxin causes the diarrheal form rather than the emetic form.
Invasion of the intestinal wall
Bacillus cereus food poisoning is a toxin effect, with symptoms due to exotoxin rather than invasion.
A neurotoxin blocking acetylcholine
Blocking acetylcholine release is botulinum toxin, which paralyzes rather than causing vomiting.
A small, heat-stable peptide
Correct: the emetic form comes from a small, heat-stable peptide; the diarrheal form comes from a large protein.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What does protective antigen do in the anthrax exotoxin?
opts: Coats the cell as a polypeptide capsule
The polypeptide capsule is a separate virulence factor that resists phagocytes, not a component of the exotoxin.
Creates a receptor site for the other two parts
Correct: protective antigen binds host cells, giving edema factor and lethal factor their receptor site, the glue of the toxin.
Impairs phagocytosis and blocks monocyte cytokines
Impairing phagocytosis and blocking tumor necrosis factor and interleukin 6 production is the work of edema factor.
Lyses macrophages, releasing a cytokine surge
Lysing macrophages at high levels, with a flood of cytokines, is the work of lethal factor.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: When does Actinomyces israelii cause disease?
opts: When it is inhaled from soil
Actinomyces israelii is an endogenous resident; disease comes from its access to deeper tissue.
When it reaches deeper tissue
Correct: normally a harmless resident of the mouth, digestive tract and genital tract, it causes chronic, hard-to-diagnose infection once it reaches deeper tissue.
Whenever it is present in the mouth
Its presence in the mouth is normal and harmless; disease follows access to deeper tissue.
When it is eaten in raw milk
Raw milk is linked to Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis, not to actinomycosis.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 93

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How is respiratory diphtheria acquired?
opts: Accidental puncture wounds with soil
Puncture wounds with soil introduce Clostridium tetani spores.
Inhaled spores from infected animal wool
Inhaled spores from wool cause pulmonary anthrax; Corynebacterium diphtheriae forms no spores.
Respiratory droplets
Correct: it is acquired via respiratory droplets from healthy carriers or actively infected people.
Contaminated dairy products and deli meat
Dairy and deli meats carry Listeria monocytogenes rather than diphtheria.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 61

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Foodborne botulism is most associated with which foods?
opts: Low-acid, home-canned vegetables
Correct: home-canned green beans and corn are the classic sources, though meats, fish and dairy can also carry it.
Cooked rice left out and reheated
Reheated rice is the classic vehicle of Bacillus cereus food poisoning.
Unpasteurized soft cheeses
Soft cheeses and dairy are the vehicles of Listeria monocytogenes.
Undercooked ground chicken
Undercooked meat and poultry are linked to listeriosis and Clostridium perfringens rather than to botulism.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 34

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which finding is characteristic of respiratory diphtheria?
opts: Raised colonic plaques
Raised plaques lining the colon are the pseudomembranes of Clostridioides difficile colitis.
A throat pseudomembrane
Correct: inflammatory fluid solidifies into a pseudomembrane, which with the swelling is indicative of the diagnosis and can cause asphyxiation.
A painless black eschar
A painless papule that becomes a black eschar is cutaneous anthrax.
Rigid arching spasms
Rigid arching spasms come from tetanospasmin in tetanus, not from diphtheria.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 62

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which is the most common form of anthrax?
opts: Gastrointestinal
Gastrointestinal anthrax follows eating contaminated meat and is far less common than the cutaneous form.
Injection
Injection anthrax has been identified in heroin-injecting addicts in northern Europe and not yet in the United States.
Cutaneous
Correct: cutaneous anthrax, acquired through cuts or incisions in the skin, accounts for the great majority of human cases.
Pulmonary
Pulmonary anthrax (woolsorters' disease) is the deadliest form rather than the most common one.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What does fecal microbiota transplant do for Clostridioides difficile infection?
opts: Delivers antitoxin directly into the colon
Fecal transplant contains donor bacteria rather than antitoxin against the enterotoxins.
Removes the pseudomembrane surgically
No tissue is removed; the transplant replaces the lost normal flora.
Vaccinates the patient against the toxin
Fecal transplant is not a vaccine; it repopulates the colon with donor flora.
Restores normal colonic flora from a donor
Correct: donor cultures are given by colonoscope or nasogastric tube, or as capsules, re-establishing the flora that keeps the organism in check.
set2.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 48
